#4906. Tokenized Nvidia market cap surges 159% amid Jensen Huang’s exit

Nvidia stock tokens reached $401.9 million in combined value as Jensen Huang stepped down and the chipmaker posted record quarterly revenue.

The combined market value of tokenized stocks tied to Nvidia shares rose about 159% from Nov. 8 to Tuesday, while the chipmaker’s Nasdaq-listed shares fell nearly 17% from their last close before co-founder Jensen Huang publicly admitted to an extramarital affair.

The value of Nvidia (NVDA) tokens tracked by Token Terminal rose from $155 million on Nov. 8 to $401.9 million by Tuesday.

Nvidia shed about $750 billion in market value, falling from $4.5 trillion at the Nov. 6 close to $3.75 trillion at Tuesday’s close, according to Yahoo Finance data.

Huang acknowledged the affair in a message to Nvidia employees on Nov. 8, nearly two weeks after The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang of spying for Beijing. China denied the allegations.

Related: ARK sells $85M in Nvidia shares ahead of chipmaker’s Q3 earnings results

Nvidia supplies chips that cloud providers such as Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure use to train and run AI models, making its earnings a gauge of global spending on AI infrastructure.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens designed to track the price of a share. In one common setup, an issuer creates tokens backed by shares held by a custodian.

Binance, for example, lists an Nvidia token that can trade when Nasdaq is closed. It gives investors exposure to Nvidia’s share price without shareholder rights. The market value can rise as more tokens enter circulation, even if Nvidia’s share price falls.

Huang resigned as president and CEO of Nvidia and stepped down from the company’s board Thursday. Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

On Tuesday, Nvidia’s board said it “does not intend to reinstate” Huang, shortly after the chipmaker reported record third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier and above Wall Street estimates. Data center sales more than doubled to $107.6 billion, accounting for about 93% of total revenue. Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter sales of about $130 billion.

Nvidia’s shares rose 2.82% to $159.80 in Wednesday premarket trading as of 12:50 pm UTC (07:50 am ET), according to Yahoo Finance.

#4902. 'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

For an AI developer, hearing that your model is nice is always pretty good. But hearing your model is like a "sadistic shinigami that turns your life into a living hell," is a totally different thing.

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Tuesday, promising smarter AI agents, better coding and impressive creative capabilities. Some of the developers who tested the models before launch had a rather different message: They're brilliant, frustrating and, in certain cases, almost impossible to work with.

The reaction quickly spilled across social media. AI engineer Hesam, who is very active in the AI community declared that “everyone agrees it’s the worst model OAI dropped.”

Developer and T3 Code creator Theo Browne published a lengthy letter to OpenAI following early testing. “I do not like 6.2 Astra. I would not choose this over Opus 5.5 for my work as a developer,” he wrote. He said OpenAI had fixed only a handful of the complaints he submitted.

“It speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands,” Theo wrote, calling its answers “the most unparsable outputs of any llm I've used this year,” referring to large language models. The complaint was as much about communication as capability: Astra could solve complex problems but struggled to explain what it had done or recognize when it was asking users questions they could not possibly answer.

In one experiment, Theo asked Astra to create a new level for Outer Wilds. Two hours into the project, the model declared itself blocked and asked: “does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?” The technical question was, from his perspective, incomprehensible and irrelevant to someone who had simply requested a playable level.

Things went worse in a code rewrite. Theo said he gave Astra seven days to improve the project; it landed no improvements and made the compiler 56% slower. Four more days yielded zero changes. “It runs in loops and goes nowhere,” he wrote.

This whole weird language issue is not isolated. For example, pseudonymous account, TokenGremlin, praised the model: “GPT-6.2 Astra is SOTA in Three.js, Blender, and 3D,” but said it “starts speaking an alien language during long workflows.”

Theo also described asking why worktrees were slow on one computer. Astra responded with four paragraphs about package-manager internals and cache behavior. The answer Theo said he received from Claude Opus 5.5 was considerably clearer.

“it's because the ssd is slow,” Claude replied.

The model's supposed creativity was another sore spot. Theo and another tester independently requested original levels for two different games, Outer Wilds and Majora's Mask. Both got water-and-bell-themed musical levels, both named “Bellwether.” “This model regresses to the mean like nothing I've ever seen,” Theo wrote.

Several other accounts also flagged the same slop: Seems like GPT-6.2 Astra has a thing for bells.

— Racist James Franco (@racist_james) November 18, 2026

For a model supposedly capable of extraordinary creativity, repeatedly inventing the same level wasn't an encouraging sign.

AI developer Matt Shumer was also disappointed. “I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad,” he wrote, arguing it might impress in small demonstrations but “just straight up doesn't work” when pushed on serious projects. In a separate follow-up he called it “utterly unusable.”

I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad.

It's fine if you're playing putt-putt golf with the models, but if you're trying to drive them the way you should be, this model just straight up doesn't work.

— Matt Shumer (@mattshumer_) November 17, 2026

Max Weinbach described the same gap between intelligence and usability. “I had more time being annoyed by the models than time I was impressed by them,” he wrote. In a follow-up, he praised the models' ability to do “fantastic work” but said they “need a ton of ‘continue’ prompts” and often stop rather than try another approach. “Using them is a struggle and annoying even if they are really good models.”

Elsewhere, an X commentator compared the previous Astra to “a sadistic shinigami” and claimed the new version only made matters worse.

6.0 astra was very like a sadistic shinigami who would make your life a living hell if you asked for any kind of help

an incredibly powerful model that somehow required you to run yourself into the ground just to get it to accomplish anything

Yet some of the same developers also praised Astra. Theo called it a “great reviewer” and “world class at 3d & game stuff,” singled out its computer-control abilities, and described a novel reverse-proxy solution he estimated could save $25,000 monthly. The split was between impressive capabilities and how difficult it was to get dependable work out of them.

Those strengths are consistent with the technical capabilities OpenAI promoted at launch. As earlier coverage detailed, independent testing placed Astra at 62 out of 100 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, an aggregate of nine evaluations covering capabilities including reasoning, coding and scientific knowledge. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scored 65.

Some of the criticism has support in OpenAI's own safety documentation.

In an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, researchers gave AI agents realistic coding tasks with deliberately introduced obstacles, such as missing files or unavailable tools. They measured the percentage of trials in which a model's final response concealed or misrepresented those obstacles.

GPT-6.2 Astra concealed the obstacle in 22.28% of those trials, versus 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra. The numbers quickly circulated on X, where AI commentator and leaker Chetaslua summarized the finding as “2x worse at telling you when it's stuck.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded publicly to the backlash. “Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with,” he wrote, promising to prioritize improvements. “But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.”

Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases.

But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.

OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux suggested early reviews may not fully reflect the version users received at launch. “We gave a few folks access a while ago and then made a lot of changes in the last 3-4 days,” he wrote, adding that he was “pretty sure no re-testing was done” during that period before review videos were produced.

Still, he acknowledged the underlying complaints. While calling the new models “a hefty jump” over their predecessors, Sottiaux said OpenAI had more work to do on “taste and niceness of use.”

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available through ChatGPT Work, Codex and OpenAI's API for eligible users. The Codex-specific changes are included at launch, but developers accessing the models directly through the API do not receive that same prompting intervention.

#4898. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley Uses Banded Chin-Ups to Build Upper-Body Strength

The supermodel’s go-to move targets your back and arms.

Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returned to the Victoria's Secret runway this year after a 16-year hiatus, but the supermodel has continued to make fitness a priority throughout her career.

“It’s really about consistency because I’m a gym girl—I’m always training and taking care of myself,” Rosie told Vogue.

The former Burberry Body face has previously cited strength training as her main form of exercise.

“I feel really strong and it's improved my posture, muscle tone, and definition,” she said to Vogue on a separate occasion.

She recently shared a workout clip of herself doing an impressive upper-body exercise—the banded chin-up—just days before the show, writing: “No days off.”

Chin-ups are a compound exercise targeting your back and arm muscles, including the latissimus dorsi (lats), biceps, and trapezius (traps).

A chin-up uses an underhand grip, with your palms facing you, while a pull-up uses an overhand grip, with your palms facing away.

Using a thicker band gives you more assistance when performing reps, while a thinner band gives you less.

Remember: while models' and celebrities' training routines can be inspiring, genetics also play a significant role in body shape, height and how easily someone builds muscle or stays lean. Take inspiration from the healthy habits – not the expectation of looking identical.

While the chin-up is a challenging movement, you can build up to your first bodyweight rep—without a band—using a few progression exercises.

Holding yourself above the bar keeps your muscles under constant tension, which helps build strength.

This exercise requires you to lower yourself as slowly as possible from the top of the movement. People are generally much stronger in the lowering phase of an exercise than in the lifting portion, making it easier than trying to pull yourself up. However, the movement still works your muscles throughout the entire range of motion, helping you build the strength needed to perform a chin-up.

Rosie has highlighted the importance of focusing on skill and feeling confident over aesthetics.

“For me, it’s really about feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape. Competence builds confidence,” she said.

Getting stronger brings her a sense of accomplishment.

“There's nothing more satisfactory to me than when I go up in weight,” she added to Vogue. “It makes me happy when I start to see the results of [consistently] lifting.” In fact, regularly working out is “when [she] feels her strongest and fittest.”

She added that motherhood had given her a new perspective on her body.

“I’m about to turn 40 next year; I look at my body and I have so much appreciation for having had two children,” Rosie continued.

Kate puts together fitness content that covers functional and strength training, cardio, workout challenges, interviews and news. She's often doing gym laundry or listening to music.

#4897. Robert Pattinson Is Officially the Next James Bond. Director James Gray Believes He Can Pull It Off.

“What Rob does have is something enigmatic about him,” Pattinson’s Lost City of Z director says. “And that enigmatic quality, I think, might serve very well for that.”

THE LONG SEARCH for a new James Bond has finally come to an end: Robert Pattinson will play the world’s most famous spy in the new installment from director Denis Villeneuve. His casting marks the conclusion of a race that not too long ago looked to be down to a trio of contenders—Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor—to go along with a “mystery candidate.” Now, the man of mystery can claim victory (Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were both revealed as late-in-the-game candidates to play 007).

Pattinson, who first achieved fame as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 before skyrocketing to another level with the Twilight franchise starting in 2008, has spent the last 15 years establishing himself as perhaps our most unique and eccentric actor, a uniquely handsome talent who seems to relish in playing a series of freaks, weirdos, and deviants. Roles in movies like Josh and Benny Safdie’s Good Time and Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse made it abundantly clear that Pattinson’s talent and ambition reach far beyond the franchises for which he initially gained recognition.

One of Pattinson’s best roles in that period came in 2016’s The Lost City of Z, an adventure film (based on the nonfiction book of the same name) from director James Gray. In Lost City, Pattinson plays Henry Costin, the eccentric assistant to Charlie Hunnam’s lead explorer Percy Fawcett.

In making Lost City of Z, Gray got an up-close opportunity to work with Pattinson and see just what he’s capable of as an actor. “The character he was playing with me—this bearded, oddball, left field explorer type—is so different from Bond,” Gray tells Men’s Health. “But that doesn’t mean he couldn’t do it. What Rob does have is something enigmatic about him. And that enigmatic quality, I think, might serve very well for that.”

Gray, who spoke with MH just a few days ahead of Pattinson’s official casting when speculation was at its peak, was fully confident in the 40-year-old’s ability to pull just about any role off, calling him a “fabulous actor,” and reflecting fondly on their time working together in the jungle.

“Look, they will know,” Gray continues. “I mean, Denis [Villeneuve] will know, he’s probably screen-tested already. I haven’t talked to him about it, but I’m sure he’s looked at all these screen tests, and it’s a thing that you know immediately when you see it on the big screen.”

Gray was onto something, as Pattinson has now officially been cast as the seventh actor to play James Bond, following in the footsteps of only Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig.

Pattinson is at the tail end of what’s been a truly remarkable year, starring in The Drama, The Odyssey, and Primetime, with a villainous supporting role in Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three still to come.

It’s also worth noting that Pattinson’s output hasn’t exclusively been weirdos and oddballs (although it is also worth noting that at one point he had a streak where his characters kept masturbating on screen in every movie). The Batman he proved he can expertly lead one of pop culture’s biggest and most valuable franchises in a way that he made totally his own (and is currently in the process of filming that film’s long-in-the-making sequel), and his role as Neil in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet may as well have been his unofficial Bond audition. Pattinson’s sleek, funny, and cool as hell as a time-traveling secret agent in that film, looking handsome and dapper along the way.

Gray himself is no stranger to talented actors; his latest film, Paper Tiger, pairs Adam Driver and Miles Teller. But he emphasizes the mere fact that Villeneuve and the film’s producers had Pattinson screen test for the role. “It means that they saw something special in him,” he says. “I’m sure he could pull it off—he’s a brilliant actor.”

#4896. How to preserve wealth and access funds during a national emergency

As geopolitical and technological threats multiply, the big question is whether you can hold on to your wealth and access funds when the system fails.

Amid kinetic war, cyberattacks and the prospect of the power grid failing, governments around the world have been encouraging citizens to prepare for major disruption.

In the UK, citizens have been stocking up on tinned food and bottled water in response to the government’s Be Ready campaign.

With fighter jets streaking across the skies of the Middle East, talk of a dirty bomb attack on Washington and the world’s largest software company going offline for a day, the possibility of disaster striking close to home is starting to look more realistic.

But what do you do with your money in times like these? How can you protect your wealth, but still be able to access it when the system fails?

There are two key aspects: choosing assets that maintain value even as the world goes up in flames, and being able to access funds during an emergency.

On the first point Maximilian Kunkel, chief investment officer for ultra-high-net-worth clients at UBS Global Wealth Management, tells Magazine, “We would caution against thinking of any single asset as ‘safe’ in all circumstances.”

Instead, he says wealthy investors should focus on building a portfolio that is “resilient across different scenarios,” with enough liquidity and diversification across asset classes, currencies and geographies.

The corporation’s 2026 global family office report, representing families with an average net worth of $2.7 billion, found 64% cited major geopolitical conflict as a concern over the next 12 months. These investors are not flocking to crypto for wealth preservation however.

Hadley Stern, head of institutions at Silence Laboratories and founder of Fidelity Digital Assets, explains that financial institutions may now place Bitcoin in the same category as gold, but it does not yet enjoy the same reputation as a safe haven.

“Gold has thousands of years of history [...] Bitcoin has less than two decades. But the reasoning people use is the same: a scarce asset that isn’t anyone else’s liability,” he says.

Related: Will gold’s ‘infinite mint bug’ make Bitcoin more valuable?

He advises against using it as a reliable hedge in a crisis; “I’d be careful with the hedge story,” he says. “Bitcoin is still volatile, and in a sell-off it often trades like other risk assets.”

Cash, by contrast, is handy for emergencies “for liquidity and paying bills,” but not for “holding value over long stretches,” he says.

Michael D’Alessio, chief operating officer at digital asset trading platform Talos, tells Magazine, there are early signs that Bitcoin is beginning to behave more like gold. He said that through the volatility around the US midterm elections Bitcoin’s correlation with equities remained high. However, over the same period, its correlation with gold also rose sharply, to around 0.75 on a 30-day basis as of early August:

BTC vs gold, 30-day rolling correlation of daily returns. Source: Talos/Coin Metrics

The collapse of Mt Gox, or more recently the failure of Paraguay’s Ueno Bank show that “the asset is only as safe as the system holding it,” according to Stern.

Rather than automatically moving into Bitcoin or gold when tensions rise, risk committees are asking different questions:

“Where is the asset? Which jurisdiction is it in? Who can freeze it? What happens if a counterparty or a payment rail is down for a week?” he says. “Those used to be back-office questions. Now they come up at the board level.”

Kunkel said that concern over major geopolitical conflict is encouraging wealthy families to consider “not only asset allocation, but also where assets are held, currency exposure, liquidity and jurisdictional diversification.”

The UBS report found that 88% of family offices hold bankable assets in two or more jurisdictions, while 30% are increasing or considering increasing currency diversification.

Related: Half of UK wealth advisers say clients’ crypto is ‘invisible’ to them: CoinShares survey

Fortunately the banks and custody providers are making practical disaster preparations too.

“Regulators expect firms to plan for severe but plausible events,” Stern explains, such as a cloud outage, a cyberattack, a key vendor failing or a market closed for days, and “show they can keep their most important services running through them.”

The UK government is advising citizens to stock up on supplies. Source: Gov.uk

For custody providers, that means testing whether assets can still be moved if a signing location goes offline, and how quickly operations can recover if a data center is lost. Stern says while households might prep for an emergency by stocking a full pantry:

Similarly investors need to work out which assets you can reach quickly and which you can’t, and “keeping enough liquidity to get through a bad stretch without being forced to sell.”

Kunkel says capital preservation “does not mean eliminating volatility, but maintaining enough liquidity and diversification to withstand volatility” without becoming a forced seller.

When the balloon goes up, diversification can protect a portfolio from a market shock, but it can’t guarantee access to funds if the infrastructure supporting it fails. A safe haven isn’t just about owning the right things; it’s about being able to access them when the system stops working.

#4895. Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.

The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.

Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.

It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.

Amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin launched using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.

With GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a new all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.

The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.

Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.

https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve

That propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a new high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.

The game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the company behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.

It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.

Those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.

"No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one."

"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS."

"It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro said in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

#4893. The 6 Best Pillows of 2026, Tested by Editors

The $190 Purple Harmony Pillow might be divisive, but it earned our best overall badge.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As someone with frequent neck pain, I would give up my cozy sheets, white noise machine, and sunrise alarm clock if it meant I wouldn’t wake up with a stiff neck. (And that’s coming from someone who invests a lot in their sleep.)

"I think that a pillow can make a big difference in people that have a history of neck issues," says Leia Rispoli, MD, an interventional pain management specialist and physiatrist at DISC Sport & Spine Center. This is the very reason why I tend to lug my favorite pillow around on weekend trips.

There isn’t one pillow that works for everyone. Your best option depends on your sleep position, preferred firmness, body type, and whether you tend to overheat at night. To find the best pillows, our editors and testers slept on popular models from Purple, Casper, Coop, Saatva, and other leading sleep brands. We evaluated each one for comfort, support, temperature regulation, adjustability, ease of care, and value.

I love the Purple Harmony Pillow so much that I try to convert nearly everyone who mentions sleep within earshot of me. I even pack it for overnight trips. But it does feel unusual at first. Inside, a springy, ventilated latex core is wrapped in Purple’s GelFlex Grid, a flexible, honeycomb-shaped layer that bends under the weight of your head and springs back when you move. Together, these materials make the pillow feel buoyant rather than sink-in like memory foam.

I tested the medium, 6.5-inch loft, meaning the pillow’s height before it is compressed. It provided enough height to support my head and neck while I slept on my side without feeling rigid. The materials give slightly beneath heavier areas, which helped reduce uncomfortable pressure around my head and neck. As someone who frequently experiences neck and back pain, I consistently felt comfortable and supported while sleeping on it.

Purple recommends the low, 5.5-inch version for most stomach and back sleepers. The medium and tall versions are generally better suited to side and combination sleepers, who often need more height to fill the space between the head and mattress. Body size and personal preference will also affect which height feels most comfortable.

The Harmony was also one of the coolest pillows I tested. Air circulates through the ventilated latex and open honeycomb layer instead of becoming trapped inside a solid block of foam. Its stretchy outer cover is also designed to draw sweat away from the skin so it can evaporate. Even on warmer nights, I rarely felt the need to flip the pillow over in search of a cooler surface.

After nearly three years of regular use, my pillow has not developed noticeable lumps or gone flat. Its durable build helps justify the high price, but there are compromises. The pillow is unusually heavy, and some sleepers may notice the grid’s texture through the cover. Purple’s 30-night trial is also shorter than the trial periods offered by many competing brands.

Still, no other pillow I tested delivered the same combination of responsive support, cooling, and long-term shape retention. I would purchase it again without hesitation.

Women’s Health art director Christine Giordano typically sleeps with two or three pillows, but the Casper Original gave her enough support to use fewer. “This pillow gave me the support I needed while still feeling light and airy,” she says. “It was breathable and didn’t clump, keeping me cool and comfortable at night.”

The Casper uses a pillow-within-a-pillow design: A firmer inner cushion provides structure, while a softer outer layer adds cushioning. Both layers are filled with polyester microfiber, a synthetic material made to feel light and fluffy like down. The construction prevented Giordano’s head from sinking too deeply while still giving the pillow a plush feel.

Giordano tries to sleep on her back but usually shifts onto her left side during the night. The pillow remained comfortable and supportive in both positions, making it a strong choice for combination sleepers who alternate between their backs and sides. However, stomach sleepers or people who prefer a flatter pillow may find its approximately nine-inch uncompressed height too lofty.

The breathable cotton cover and airy synthetic fill also prevented the pillow from feeling stuffy during testing. It’s not as breathable as a dedicated cooling pillow, but Giordano did not notice heat buildup or need to flip it over for a cooler surface.

The entire pillow is machine-washable, which makes it easier to clean than models with foam or latex cores. Its soft filling may need occasional fluffing to maintain its shape, but Giordano did not notice clumping during testing.

At under $100, it is one of the more affordable pillows we tested. Giordano liked it enough that she replaced some of the other pillows in her home and purchased additional Casper ones for her family.

Women’s Health executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, calls the Coop Original Adjustable the most comfortable pillow she has tried. “I’ve never been a pillow snob or had major issues with basic pillows from Amazon, but I noticed that this was far more comfortable than other, cheaper pillows I’ve used,” she says.

The pillow is filled with a blend of shredded memory foam and microfiber. Memory foam molds around the head and neck, while the soft synthetic fibers keep the pillow from feeling like a dense, solid block of foam. Unlike a pillow with a fixed height, the Coop can be unzipped so you can remove filling for a flatter feel or add more for extra support. The process can get messy, but that adjustability makes it easier to tailor the pillow to your body and sleep position.

Coop offers the pillow in classic, crescent, and cut-out shapes. Andriakos tested the classic and cut-out versions while switching between side and stomach sleeping. She preferred the cut-out, which has a curved indentation that creates room for the shoulder and allows the pillow to sit closer to the neck.

“I liked that it could wrap around my neck and shoulders, and I could almost cuddle it like a body pillow with an arm threaded underneath,” she says. Although the shape can look slightly awkward inside a standard pillowcase, it was super comfortable when she slept on her side.

The pillow felt plush, but Andriakos’ head did not sink so deeply that her neck felt unsupported. She also found the outer cover breathable, although sleepers who regularly overheat may prefer a pillow specifically designed for cooling.

Because its height can be adjusted, the Coop can work for side, back, stomach, and combination sleepers. Side sleepers will generally need more filling to keep the head level with the spine, while stomach sleepers may prefer to remove enough filling to create a flatter surface. Finding the right amount may require a few nights of experimentation, but Coop’s 100-night trial gives you time to make those adjustments.

It would take an exceptional pillow for me to consider replacing my Purple Harmony, but the Saatva Latex Pillow gave it serious competition. Although both pillows contain latex, they feel noticeably different. Purple uses one solid, springy latex core, while Saatva uses shredded pieces of latex surrounded by a soft layer of fine synthetic fibers. This gives the Saatva a plusher, more traditional feel, but it has enough structure to support the head and neck.

The pillow feels dense when you first pick it up, but my head settled gently into the soft outer layer without sinking too deeply. The shredded latex inside quickly returned to its original shape when I moved, so the pillow stayed supportive as I shifted positions. As a side sleeper who frequently experiences neck pain, I did not wake up with additional stiffness.

Saatva offers two heights. The standard version measures approximately four to five inches and is designed for back and stomach sleepers who generally need a lower pillow. The high-loft version measures approximately six to seven inches and is better suited to side and combination sleepers who need more height between their heads and mattresses.

I also appreciated that the pillow remained breathable throughout the night. The small spaces between the pieces of shredded latex allow air to circulate, while the cotton cover feels cool. It does not create the immediately cold sensation of a cooling pillow, but I did not notice uncomfortable heat buildup.

The outer layer is filled with microdenier fibers, which are very fine synthetic strands designed to imitate the light, fluffy feel of down. You can machine-wash this outer layer and its cotton cover, but the inner latex core must be removed and kept out of the washing machine.

At $165 for a standard/queen size, this is one of the more expensive pillows we tested. Saatva also provides only 45 days for returns, which is shorter than the trial periods offered by several competitors. Still, its combination of plush cushioning, responsive support, and breathable materials makes it an excellent choice for sleepers who want a luxury-hotel feel that’s still supportive.

For hot sleepers, a breathable pillow can be the difference between a good night’s sleep and a night spent tossing and turning. The Slumber Cloud UltraCool stood out because its cooling effect was immediately noticeable during testing.

Women’s Health managing editor Laura McLaughlin described the sensation as “a little sci-fi” because the surface felt immediately cool when she rested her head on it. The cover contains Outlast, a material designed to absorb excess body heat when you become warm and release it as your skin cools. This helps prevent heat from collecting around your head and face, although the effect may be less noticeable beneath a thick pillowcase.

McLaughlin also found the pillow easy to combine with others. “It’s great for layering with other pillows to get just the right height,” she says. “It’s neither too dense nor too high to use in combination with others already in place.” That makes it especially useful for sleepers who want additional height without placing a rigid pillow beneath their heads.

The interior is filled with polyester down alternative, a synthetic material designed to imitate the airy feel of down. It is available in soft/medium and medium/firm versions, allowing sleepers to choose how plush or structured they want the pillow to feel. The softer option will generally suit stomach sleepers or anyone who prefers more sink while the firmer version may provide better support for back and side sleepers.

The entire pillow can be machine-washed, a convenient advantage over pillows with foam or latex cores. However, synthetic filling can begin to clump after repeated use and washing, so it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the material.

Although the UltraCool does not provide the customized support of an adjustable pillow, it delivered the most noticeable cooling sensation of any model we tested.

The Brooklinen Down Alternative Pillow is built for sleepers who want the fluffy feel of down without actual feathers. It’s filled with recycled poly microgel, a cluster of fine synthetic fibers that creates a light cushioning similar to down.

Unlike many pillows that come in only one firmness, this one is available in soft, medium, and firm versions. Brooklinen recommends the soft pillow for stomach sleepers who generally need less height beneath the head; the medium for back sleepers; and the firm for side sleepers who typically need more support to fill the space between the head and mattress.

Its cotton sateen shell feels smooth and has a subtle sheen. The pillow is also certified by OEKO-TEX Standard 100, which means its materials have been tested for a list of regulated substances. That certification does not evaluate the pillow’s comfort, durability, or environmental impact.

Brooklinen allows most products to be returned within 365 days, although it deducts a $9.95 return fee from the refund. That’s one of the most generous return windows we’ve seen.

The pillow can be machine-washed in cold water and tumble-dried on low with wool dryer balls until completely dry. As with most pillows filled with loose synthetic fibers, it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the fill and preserve its shape.

A pillow’s height, or loft, should keep your head and neck aligned with your spine. Side sleepers generally need a taller pillow, back sleepers a medium-height pillow, and stomach sleepers a low pillow. Your mattress matters, too: The more deeply your shoulders sink into it, the less pillow height you may need. Most of the pillows we tested fell in the five- to nine-inch range, offering different levels of support depending on their material and sleeping position.

Side sleepers often benefit from a medium-firm or firm pillow that maintains its height. Back sleepers generally need medium support while stomach sleepers may prefer something softer that compresses easily. Because firmness labels vary by brand, consider the pillow’s material and height as well.

“There isn't one brand that's the magical brand for everyone,” says Rispoli. Look for a pillow that supports your head without tilting your neck sharply upward or downward. Adjustable pillows can help you fine-tune the height. Consult a health care professional if your pain is persistent, severe, or accompanied by numbness or weakness.

Memory foam molds around the head but may retain heat. Latex feels springy, breathable, and durable. Down is soft and airy but may lack structure while synthetic down alternative is usually easier to wash but may flatten over time. Hybrid pillows combine materials to balance cushioning and support.

Look for ventilated latex, shredded filling, or another construction that allows air to circulate. Some covers also absorb excess body heat or feel cool, although a thick pillowcase may reduce the effect. People who sleep cold may prefer denser foam or plush down filling that holds slightly more warmth.

As a sleep writer, I’ve tested all kinds of sleep accessories, from mattresses to eye masks, but pillows are probably my most-tested product category. (Unfortunately, I once tested so many pillows at the same time that I injured my neck, but I’ve learned my lesson.) To find the best pillows available online, I selected popular picks from leading sleep brands, like Purple, Casper, Saatva, Pluto, and more, for testing. Some helpful testers and I have slept on these pillows for dozens of nights to determine whether they’re worth the money, and our top pick has been my favorite pillow to sleep on for nearly three years. From flat pillow lovers to hot sleepers, our diverse crew of sleepers tried out eight pillows of various styles, materials, and price points.

#4889. Fed's Waller Calls for 50-Basis-Point Rate Hike, Says Tokenized Finance Still Needs Traditional Banks

Fed's Waller Calls for 50-Basis-Point Rate Hike, Says Tokenized Finance Still Needs Traditional Banks

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller wants the central bank to get more aggressive with interest rate hikes, arguing that stubborn inflation may require a 50-basis-point increase in December rather than the smaller move investors expect.

Speaking during a CNBC interview Wednesday, Waller said the Fed must either deliver a half-percentage-point increase at its December 8-9 meeting or explicitly signal that another hike will follow in January.

“You might need to, like, shock people,” Waller said, referring to the central bank's efforts to prevent businesses and consumers from accepting inflation near 3% as normal.

“My view is then you have to go 50 in December to put it in place and get it done,” he said, warning that insufficiently aggressive action could weaken expectations that inflation will return to the Fed's target.

Waller's concerns follow three consecutive months in which core consumer prices rose 0.3%, a pace equivalent to roughly 3.5% inflation annually. That's considerably higher than the Fed's 2% target, which is formally measured using a separate inflation indicator known as the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index.

The governor had already established his threshold for a more aggressive move in a November 10 speech. He said another 0.3% core CPI reading would warrant considering a half-point hike, arguing that moving only 25 basis points could damage the Fed's credibility.

October inflation subsequently met that condition. Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% during the month, while core inflation climbed 0.3%, both exceeding economists' forecasts.

Waller's latest comments suggest he is increasingly concerned about the psychology of inflation, particularly the risk that companies begin treating annual price increases of 3% as acceptable and routinely pass higher costs to customers.

The proposed increase would lift the Fed's benchmark rate from its current range of 3.75%-4% to 4.25%-4.50%. Two consecutive quarter-point hikes in December and January would reach the same destination, but Waller argues that timing and communication matter when inflation expectations are at risk.

Markets remain less convinced that the Fed will move that aggressively in December. Futures pricing Wednesday morning showed roughly a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point increase and only about a 5% probability of a half-point move

The prospect of higher borrowing costs has been particularly painful for crypto investors. Higher interest rates make Treasury securities and other interest-bearing investments more competitive with speculative assets, while tighter financial conditions can reduce the money available for riskier bets.

Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp selloff amid the changing rate outlook. As Decrypt previously covered, persistent inflation fears have coincided with withdrawals from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and weakening technical indicators, adding pressure to an already fragile market.

Waller's increasingly hawkish monetary-policy stance comes alongside a more accommodating view of blockchain networks, although he sees established financial infrastructure as essential to its adoption.

In a separate November 17 speech at The Clearing House Annual Conference in New York, Waller discussed how tokenization—the representation of financial assets on digital networks—could reshape payments and securities markets. That speech focused on financial technology rather than interest-rate policy.

He pointed to a growing convergence between traditional markets and blockchain platforms, with banks and payment providers experimenting with tokenized deposits, stablecoins, and programmable transactions.

Waller described how tokenized money could allow investors to purchase securities outside conventional trading hours, with payments and assets changing hands simultaneously through smart contracts.

But he rejected the idea that the development of blockchain-based markets necessarily makes existing payment infrastructure obsolete.

“Central bank money need not be used in every transaction or on every platform, but its presence at the foundation of the system is essential,” Waller said.

#4887. Sanctions fears loom over Russia’s regulated crypto trading launch

Russia’s crypto trading rollout faces uncertainty as companies weigh sanctions exposure, while Moscow Exchange prepares to launch crypto trading in December.

Russia’s push to bring cryptocurrency trading under government oversight is raising concerns that greater transparency could expose market participants to international sanctions.

Some companies are reluctant to join the Bank of Russia’s public registry of crypto exchangers because they fear becoming sanctions targets, a person familiar the regulatory discussions told Cointelegraph on Wednesday.

Industry representatives repeatedly asked the central bank to keep the registry private, but the regulator refused, arguing that crypto businesses should follow the same requirements as traditional financial service providers, the source said.

The concerns come as the European Union prepares its 22nd sanctions package against Russia, which is expected to include new restrictions on crypto platforms.

Russia’s new rules allowing retail investors to buy Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and Tether’s USDt (USDT) took effect on Monday, and the central bank’s registry listed 30 authorized exchange operators as of Wednesday.

The list includes major lenders Sberbank and VTB, but registration alone does not establish whether customers can already complete transactions.

Related: KuCoin suspends services in Russia and Belarus

Alexander Nam of HSE University’s Center for Decentralized Finance and Digital Financial Assets Research said the market still faces technical and regulatory hurdles, including investor testing, order execution, settlement and custody.

“Being included in the registry does not in itself mean readiness to fully serve investors,” Nam told Cointelegraph.

Alexander Brazhnikov of the Russian Association of Cryptocurrency and Blockchain told Cointelegraph that he could not identify a registered operator offering confirmed retail access as of Monday.

Moscow Exchange (MOEX), Russia’s main securities trading venue, plans to launch crypto trading on Dec. 1, with investors accessing the market through brokers rather than directly through the exchange. Cointelegraph contacted VTB, T-Invest Lab and MOEX for further details on their respective crypto trading launch plans but had not received responses by publication time.

The European Commission reportedly plans to present its next sanctions package ahead of a Nov. 26–27 European Council summit, days before MOEX’s scheduled launch.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Western sanctions had backfired and strengthened Russia’s economy, speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

Russia’s broader crypto activity has declined despite its push to establish a regulated trading market. The value of cryptocurrency transactions fell 14.7% to $284.1 billion in the year ended June 2026, according to Chainalysis. The country still accounted for roughly 44% of Eastern Europe’s crypto activity.

#4883. CoinShares sells all treasury ETH, halves SOL holdings for buybacks

The October sales raised $19.3 million, nearly half the $40 million CoinShares can spend on buybacks before its next annual meeting.

European digital asset manager CoinShares sold its entire Ether treasury position and half of its Solana treasury holdings in October, raising $19.3 million to fund share buybacks.

CoinShares raised $16.6 million from the Ether sale and $2.7 million from the Solana sale, the company said in its third-quarter results on Wednesday.

CoinShares reported treasury holdings of 6,562 Ether (ETH) at a fair value of $17.6 million and 50,213 Solana (SOL) valued at $5.9 million as of Sept. 30. The company also held 235 Bitcoin (BTC) worth $19.6 million at quarter-end.

CoinShares’ board approved up to $40 million in buybacks on Oct. 22 under a five-year authorization that shareholders granted in September. The authorization covers up to 32.9 million shares, or 25% of shares outstanding. The $40 million program runs until the company’s next annual meeting, expected in the second quarter of 2027.

“That’s nearly half of the $40 million authorized by the Board and gives us the flexibility to act when conditions allow,” said Jean-Marie Mognetti, co-founder, president and CEO of CoinShares, referring to the sale proceeds in a Wednesday press release.

CoinShares also reported $7.4 billion in total assets under management, up from $5.5 billion at the end of June, driven by rising crypto prices and $125 million in net inflows during the quarter. Revenue fell 45% from a year earlier to $27.7 million, including $19.1 million in asset management fees.

CoinShares’ shares fell 5.41% to close at $3.15 on Tuesday, ahead of the earnings report, leaving them down 63% from their $8.61 close on the company’s April 1 Nasdaq debut.

#4880. Bitcoin Miners Are Selling Their Stacks to Fund the AI Boom

Bitcoin Miners Are Selling Their Stacks to Fund the AI Boom

Two of the biggest U.S. Bitcoin miners are turning their Bitcoin into AI infrastructure.

MARA sold 13,597 BTC after the end of September at an average price of about $81,039, raising roughly $1.1 billion, according to its third-quarter shareholder letter filed with the SEC.

That’s about 40% of the 34,012 BTC it held at the end of September. Combined with the 26,984 BTC it sold in the first nine months of the year, MARA has sold more than 40,000 BTC in 2026, worth roughly $2.5 billion at today’s prices.

MARA used $750 million of the proceeds to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans it took out to fund its acquisition of the Long Ridge power plant.

The company said it intends to keep using Bitcoin to raise cash for AI infrastructure, convertible note puts that become exercisable next year and potential share buybacks. Its board has authorized a repurchase of up to $500 million.

MARA insisted the shift is “not a pivot away from bitcoin,” describing mining as its operating foundation while it builds out AI and high-performance computing infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Riot Platforms sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of the year for about $1.5 billion, primarily to fund data center development, and ended September with just 2,418 BTC, according to its Nov. 4 results.

The miner also signed a 15-year lease for its entire Corsicana, Texas, campus, covering 910 megawatts of capacity and worth about $28 billion over the initial term. CEO Jason Les called it “the largest lease in Riot’s history.” Riot’s quarterly filing identifies the tenant as Anthropic.

Mining economics help explain the shift. Riot’s Bitcoin mining revenue fell to $116 million in the third quarter from $160.8 million a year earlier, as the average value of each Bitcoin it mined dropped to $70,855 from $114,361.

Including equipment depreciation, Riot said it cost $78,805 to mine each Bitcoin, more than the coin’s average value over the quarter. MARA’s revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million.

The sales add supply to an already fragile market. Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said Tuesday that the two miners drove the recent selling by Bitcoin treasury companies, and that treasury firms outside those two were net buyers in November.

Strategy, the largest corporate holder, kept buying, adding 485 BTC last week to bring its holdings to 850,849 BTC, worth around $54 billion.

Bitcoin Tanks Ahead of Anthropic’s IPO. Should We Really Blame AI?

Bitcoin fell toward $63,000 Wednesday, extending a six-week retreat just as AI developer Anthropic prepared to price one of Wall Street’s biggest initial public offerings.

The timing has revived an attractive theory: investors are selling crypto to buy AI shares.

Right now Bitcoin is about to touch $62,000, down 3.8% on today’s session. Anthropic expects to price shares Wednesday at an indicated $70 to $78, ahead of Thursday’s Nasdaq debut under ANT, potentially valuing the company at $1.4 trillion, according to its IPO prospectus.

Kraken chief economist Thomas Perfumo told MarketWatch the IPO “could also be drawing capital out of risk assets” as investors position for the sale.

That’s a theory Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared, flagging the listing as one possible factor in Bitcoin’s decline in an X post Sunday.

No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation. Here are some potential reasons.

Money shifting to the Anthropic IPO: https://t.co/jYwVi4huAY

ETF outflows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.9 billion in outflows over seven trading… pic.twitter.com/XL2aB1ZL9W

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 15, 2026

There is a tempting precedent. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX listed in June and 23% in the equivalent period before Anthropic. But the comparison misses an important difference: AI stocks rallied before SpaceX; this time they have been falling alongside crypto.

“This time, the sell-off has been led by the AI trade itself,” Block Scholes research analyst Thahbib Rahman wrote in comments shared with Decrypt. Over the prior 50 days, Nvidia fell 32% and the Nasdaq dropped 11%, unlike their gains ahead of SpaceX’s IPO.

Bitcoin’s 30-day correlation with Nvidia rose from 0.20 to 0.56, while its correlation with gold fell from 0.63 to 0.39. “Liquidity is ebbing and flowing out of crypto and equities together once more,” Rahman wrote.

Bitcoin’s daily chart looks weak without any IPO theory. The relative strength index reads 21.8, well below the 30 threshold commonly associated with oversold markets, while an average directional index of 38.7 indicates a strong trend—in this case, downward.

The 50-day exponential moving average is also below its 200-day counterpart, a bearish configuration associated with the so-called death cross. The pattern historically signals deteriorating momentum and the possibility of further losses, although it is a lagging indicator and does not necessarily predict where prices will go next.

Also, oversold does not necessarily mean the selling has ended.

The immediate floor is around $62,000, close to Sunday’s low. Glassnode data show buyers absorbed 66,000 BTC between $62,000 and $66,000 during heavy selling, but stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days. Below $62,000, the next psychological level is $60,000; resistance sits near $65,500, $69,300 and $73,700.

More tangible selling pressure has already been recorded. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $239.9 million Tuesday, including $209.5 million from BlackRock’s IBIT. Nearly $2 billion in leveraged crypto bets were liquidated during the weekend rout, amplifying losses as exchanges forcibly closed positions.

Hilbert Group portfolio manager Jesse Marre called the selloff “simply a stop loss run,” arguing that derivatives traders had already capitulated. Rising Treasury yields, a stronger dollar, and renewed expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes also make speculative assets less attractive.

In other words, the dip is more natural market moves than money switching markets.

Nvidia forecast $130 billion in fourth-quarter sales, beating expectations after Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure. Yet markets remained split: global shares slipped 0.1%, while the Nasdaq gained 0.35% early and CoreWeave dropped 5.4%.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes sees the IPO less as a drain than a barometer. “Bitcoin’s going to go up too” if Anthropic soars, he said, while a weak debut could deepen pressure across risk assets.

Anthropic is scheduled to price Wednesday and start trading Thursday. Before that debut, Bitcoin must hold the same $62,000 area buyers defended during Sunday’s liquidation wave.

#4874. Bitcoin Covenants Part 6: FE Covenants — Enforcing covenants through cryptographically restricted signing keys

FE covenants encode spending constraints into the signing key, so only transactions that satisfy a predefined condition can be signed.

This is Part 6 in the technical article series about Bitcoin covenants by Cointelegraph Research. To read the previous article, click here.

Changing Bitcoin’s consensus rules is not merely a technical process. It requires that the network’s node operators, miners, developers and economic actors coordinate around a change. This coordination is difficult to achieve, which is why Bitcoin’s base layer has gradually ossified.

Researchers have spent the last several years investigating whether covenant behavior could be enforced without touching consensus rules. In May 2024, Jeremy Rubin, the original author of the OP_CTV proposal (BIP-119), offered an answer in a paper titled FE’d Up Covenants. His design proposed using functional encryption (FE) to move the covenant out of Bitcoin Script and into the signing key.

In ordinary public-key cryptography, a private key can sign any message. In hypothetical FE-based covenants, signing would be restricted to a predefined set of valid transactions. Bitcoin nodes would verify the signature with OP_CHECKSIG exactly as they do today, obviating the need for a soft fork.

Functional encryption (FE) generalizes public-key encryption. In ordinary cryptographic schemes, a private key can be used to fully decrypt a ciphertext and arrive at the plaintext. In FE, a master secret is instead used to issue subsidiary functional keys, each of which reveals only one chosen function of the plaintext. The holder of the functional key for a function f and the ciphertext of a secret x can compute f(x) but never gets to reveal x as a plaintext message.

In the academic literature, FE was first formalized by Dan Boneh, Amit Sahai and Brent Waters in 2011. Constructions for arbitrary functions followed from 2013, with polynomial runtime but overheads far beyond the resources of current computing technology. Furthermore, their security rested on new, untested building blocks called multilinear maps. Only in 2021 did researchers develop constructions from well-founded cryptographic assumptions, which could in principle open the door to practical implementations of FE.

The f in an FE scheme can be any feasibly computable function. However, in Bitcoin covenant constructions, f is a signing function. Its output is a Bitcoin signature for a transaction tx. Because this signature depends on both a private key and the transaction that is being signed, it takes at least two inputs, which is why Rubin’s design uses multi-input FE. For a covenant that only permits a single spending transaction, akin to OP_CTV, two inputs suffice. General, expressive constructions take more arguments, as in Rubin’s f(k, tx, program, proof).

Crucially, f does not sign directly with the private key k that is supplied in an encrypted form. Instead, the function derives a new key pair by tweaking k with a hash of the covenant’s spending policy. Signatures produced by f are valid for the tweaked public key, not for the base public key P itself.

To enable FE-based covenants from these primitives, a setup authority is required. It generates a Bitcoin key pair (the private key k and the public key P) as well as an FE key pair (the master secret msk and the FE public key mpk). It publishes P, mpk, k encrypted to mpk, and the functional key for f, which it derives from msk. The setup authority then needs to be trusted to destroy k and msk. Otherwise, it could sign spends that violate the covenant. With this setup completed, an indefinite number of new covenants may be created.

Every covenant has its own dedicated key pair, obtained by tweaking (k, P) with the spending policy. The private key of this tweaked key pair exists only inside f and is never revealed. The public key can be derived from P by anyone who knows the hash of the desired spending policy. This way, covenant receiving addresses can be generated. In practice, the receiving address would commit to a 2-of-2 script that requires a signature from a key the user controls alongside the FE signature. This is to keep unauthorized parties from triggering a transaction permitted by the covenant.

To create an FE signature for a covenant spend, the signer takes a tx that conforms to the spending policy and encrypts it to mpk. Using the encrypted tx, together with the encrypted k and the functional key published by the authority, they can then evaluate f. The function f signs tx with k tweaked by the hash of the spending policy. A transaction that breaks the spending policy of the address that holds the coins could at best be signed for some other, differently tweaked public key that does not control the funds.The function f can also be designed to block such a signature outright.

The general version of FE-based covenants with f(k, tx, program, proof) is strictly more expressive than OP_CTV. The general function proposed by Rubin takes a program that checks a condition on the transaction at spend time, and a zero-knowledge proof that the program accepts the transaction.

This zero-knowledge proof facilitates the implementation of the FE scheme, but does not add to it conceptually. A single fixed f works either way. Without the proof, f would have to be a general interpreter that runs any given program on tx itself. Such an f is large and costly to evaluate under FE. With the proof, f only has to verify a succinct proof. This could make it possible to enforce arbitrarily complex covenants without the need for more complexity in f. The proof also lets a spending policy depend on data outside the transaction, such as the result of an off-chain computation.

Goldwasser et al. (2014) introduced multi-input FE and built it on indistinguishability obfuscation. Multi-input FE and obfuscation are known to imply one another. Ananth and Jain (2015) showed that even single-input FE for general circuits yields obfuscation once it is made compact. The cryptographic primitive this design needs is therefore at least as hard to build as so-called indistinguishability obfuscation itself. Implementations of this principle remain at toy scale.

Carmer, Malozemoff and Raykova (2017) needed 3.7 hours to obfuscate a 12-bit pseudorandom function, a toy circuit of about 62,000 gates with a 64-bit key, far smaller than ECDSA signing on 256-bit numbers. The obfuscated program took 120 GB of disk space, and an evaluation ran for 67 minutes with 128 GB of RAM. The cost of implementing such a scheme would fall on whoever produces the signature, not on Bitcoin nodes. The authors called this “still far from practical.”

Furthermore, FE schemes that are practical cover only narrow function classes, such as the inner products of Abdalla et al. (2015), and the type of ECDSA signing required for Bitcoin covenants is not among them. Rubin’s paper concedes this point and lists under-developed cryptography and the setup trust assumption among its downsides. CTV-style opcodes remain far more efficient in bytes and verification, but require a base-layer change.

In our next article, we turn to Un-FE’d Covenants, which Rubin proposed to approximate covenant behavior without relying on impractical FE schemes. It replaces FE with oracle signers bonded through BitVM. [alloc]init’s Bitcoin PIPEs began in 2024 as an FE design and moved in 2026 to witness encryption. This proposal will also be covered in a follow-up article.

#4871. Why CoinShares Just Sold All Its Ethereum and Half Its Solana

Why CoinShares Just Sold All Its Ethereum and Half Its Solana

CoinShares, one of Europe’s largest digital-asset managers, has sold its entire corporate treasury holding of Ethereum and half of its Solana.

It’s a move that might look like a loss of conviction but is really about something more prosaic: funding a stock buyback.

The decision, disclosed Tuesday in the firm’s third-quarter results, freed up $19.3 million, comprising $16.6 million from the Ethereum sale and $2.7 million from offloading half its Solana.

That covers nearly half of the $40 million share-repurchase program the Jersey-based firm’s board approved in October, and the company was explicit that the proceeds are being “reallocating that capital towards share repurchases.”

CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti framed it as capital discipline rather than a bearish call. “We took the same approach to preparing for the share repurchase program,” he said, noting the sales give the company “the flexibility to act when conditions allow.”

In other words, CoinShares is converting idle treasury crypto into dry powder to buy back its own stock, which it can do under an authorization allowing repurchases of up to 25% of shares outstanding over five years.

The timing is notable. The sale lands during a brutal stretch for crypto markets. Bitcoin was trading around $63,200 on Wednesday, down from six-figure levels earlier in the cycle, while Ethereum sat near $1,770 and Solana around $74, both well off their recent highs.

Spot Ethereum ETFs, meanwhile, have bled cash for days, shedding $29.1 million on Nov. 17 to extend a multi-day outflow streak that has turned Decrypt’s ETF sentiment gauge “bearish.”

Those are precisely the risk-off conditions that have battered Bitcoin treasury firms and pressured the broader sector. For a company whose stock is poised to join the Russell indices in December, deploying capital into buybacks at depressed prices is a conventional play, even if the optics of a crypto manager selling crypto invite a second look.

In terms of scale, these were small corporate treasury positions, not client assets. CoinShares’ total assets under management recovered to $7.4 billion by quarter-end, up from $5.5 billion three months earlier, and its core business of digital-asset investment products is untouched by the treasury move.

The firm actually swung to a strong quarter, posting $39.6 million in net income as net inflows accelerated to $125 million and its lending and trading desks rebounded.

So the sale isn’t CoinShares souring on Ethereum or Solana, assets it still manages billions in on behalf of clients. It’s a treasury-management decision by a newly profitable, soon-to-be-index-listed company choosing to return capital to shareholders rather than let a modest crypto position sit on its balance sheet.

Data from TradingView showed Bitcoin (BTC) trading down 3% on the day, having incrementally sold off in the hours prior to the US trading session.

BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The weakness accompanied commentary on future Federal Reserve financial policy by governor Christopher Waller. Speaking to CNBC, Waller argued the case for hiking interest rates by 50 basis points at the December meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) — more than the current market consensus of 25 basis points.

With CPI inflation above the Fed’s 2% target for five years, he warned that businesses were becoming comfortable passing on 3% annual price rises “or higher” to consumers.

“You might need to, like, shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute; 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward,’” he said.

Waller described the need for “aggressive actions” to tackle inflationary trends, which he noted were spreading into areas not directly impacted by current geopolitical catalysts — the US-Iran war and associated spike in oil prices.

The latest data from CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed markets still overwhelmingly favoring a 25-basis-point hike in December, with the odds of that outcome above 95%.

Fed target-rate probabilities by FOMC meeting (screenshot). Source: CME Group

“I don’t think any of the hawks on the FOMC have made a convincing case that underlying inflation - taking supply shocks out - is running hot,” he wrote in analysis on Tuesday. Brooks described the prospect of further rate hikes as a “terrible mistake.”

Nasdaq Composite Index one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Bitcoin remained without an upside catalyst, seeking to break down from a trading range between $64,000 and $66,000 in place since Nov. 15.

Independent analyst David Eng warned that sell-side pressure remains “extreme” at current price levels. Eng cited $8.7 billion in capital outflows over the past 30 days, along with net outflows of $2.1 billion from the US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETF) year-to-date.

“Bitcoin doesn’t need another $8.7 billion of buying every month to recover. It needs the balance between buying and selling to improve. At the current 30-day pace, a $290M/day improvement would eliminate the measured net outflow,” he argued on X.

#4866. Google's Genie 4 Is Here, Letting Ultra Subscribers Build AI Worlds in Real Time

The company announced Wednesday that its latest world model is rolling out through Project Genie, a browser-based experiment for generating interactive environments. Genie 4 was unveiled in October, but access until now had been limited to trusted testers.

Instead of rendering a finished video from a prompt, Genie generates the scene as someone explores it. With the fourth model, users can type instructions midway through a session to change the weather, introduce a character, or steer what's happening without starting over.

Genie 4 also creates sound alongside the visuals, from wind and footsteps to dialogue that reacts to events in the scene. Google says the model improves the way people move and objects respond to physical forces, though those claims come from its own demonstrations rather than independent testing.

Genie has come a long way from the side-scrolling experiments Google showed in 2024. The first version learned from more than 200,000 hours of gameplay footage and could turn a single image into a simple playable 2D environment, as Decrypt reported at the time.

Those early sessions lasted just 60 seconds, and character controls or physical behavior could be unreliable. Google is now keeping Genie 3 available alongside the new model, with sessions extended to three minutes, support for 360-degree panorama images, and the ability to connect multiple generated worlds into longer journeys.

That three-minute limit applies to the updated Genie 3 experience; Google did not specify a comparable session length for Genie 4 in Wednesday's announcement. Users can choose between the models depending on whether they want Genie 4's stronger visuals and audio or Genie 3's longer explorations.

The technology is not the same as a traditional game engine that builds a stable level with fully defined rules. Genie predicts what a world should look and sound like as it changes.

Google acknowledges that objects can drift or change between views, complex physics remain difficult, and generated speech or text may be inaccurate. It says Project Genie's audio and video carry SynthID watermarks and that inputs and outputs undergo safety screening.

#4864. Palmer Luckey Says He’s Building an Offshore Haven for Industry—And 'Illegal' Medicine

Palmer Luckey Says He’s Building an Offshore Haven for Industry—And 'Illegal' Medicine

Palmer Luckey, the billionaire founder of Oculus and defense technology company Anduril, is spending over a billion dollars to have a private island where he can do things without worrying about U.S. laws.

He wants to build a massive industrial platform in the ocean where American businesses can operate without some of the regulations they face on land. And he has apparently been working on the idea for nearly a decade.

In an X post published Wednesday, Luckey revealed a project called SLAB, a proposed seastead with a 1,000-year design life that he says could support industries ranging from metal processing and oil refining to medical research and treatment.

Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.

The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,… pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF

— Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026

His goal, he wrote, is to create an industrial base cheaper than land and free from state and local laws that he believes are crippling critical American industries. Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen the United States rather than escape it, calling it a "relief valve" for outdated regulations.

“Me and a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017, and while it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion,” he wrote.

Luckey said he used proceeds from Facebook's 2014 acquisition of Oculus to finance the project.

The announcement included an AI-generated illustration of a gigantic offshore platform, rather than photographs of an operating facility so it’s hard to know which type of endeavor he’s dedicating his time and money to.

Luckey said he decided to disclose SLAB after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He rejected that characterization as incomplete, saying the project was considerably older and "way cooler than that."

Luckey provided a more specific indication of his ambitions in a heated exchange with journalist Joshua Topolsky, who questioned whether creating an offshore community was a sensible way to modernize medical research.

Topolsky argued that regulatory reform could happen without constructing an island in the ocean and challenged Luckey to identify which existing rules had prevented him from pursuing medical advances.

Luckey responded that he would rather build a place where people could save their families with "safe but currently illegal medicine ASAP" than wait for lawmakers to reform the system.

He accused political interests and large pharmaceutical companies of obstructing change, arguing that conventional reform would require legislation capable of securing support from 60 senators.

Luckey's plan also faces a significant legal complication: moving an operation into the ocean does not automatically place it outside American jurisdiction.

When another X user asked how close SLAB could operate to San Francisco without falling under its jurisdiction, Luckey answered, "Three miles."

That generally corresponds to the boundary of California's state-controlled coastal waters, according to the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management.

That said, federal jurisdiction extends considerably farther. The United States has a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea and a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, where it retains authority over certain economic activities and the construction and use of artificial islands, according to NOAA guidance.

The applicable rules would depend on SLAB's location, whether it floats or is attached to the seabed, and how it is registered. Even vessels operating on the high seas remain subject to applicable maritime laws and the jurisdiction of their flag states, so it’s not as if he’d be living in an anarchist fairy tale.

Medical research presents its own complications, if that’s what he’s actually doing. The FDA requires foreign clinical studies submitted in support of U.S. drug approvals to meet good clinical practice standards, including independent ethical review and informed consent. Conducting treatment offshore would not, by itself, make an unapproved drug legal for sale in the United States.

Previous seasteading experiments have encountered similar jurisdictional disputes. A floating community off Thailand triggered a confrontation with authorities in 2019, while a subsequent project in Panama adopted boat registration to operate within an existing legal framework.

This is all, of course, speculation. Luckey has not publicly identified SLAB's proposed location, the specific regulations it would avoid, or the medical treatments he hopes to make available. He has also not announced a construction deadline or provided independently verifiable details of the project's current physical development.

#4862. $25M Ethereum MEV acquittal tests criminal enforcement limits

BlackRock’s staked Ether ETF earns a cut of what traders pay for priority on Ethereum, the acquittal left the legal risk to that income unresolved.

BlackRock’s staked Ether ETF earns a share of what traders pay to get one Ethereum transaction ahead of another.

That income is why BlackRock flagged the prosecution of Anton and James Peraire-Bueno in its prospectus. If profiting from the order of trades were found unlawful, the firm warned, its staking program could be disrupted.

The brothers’ acquittal left that risk unresolved because the fraud case turned on a narrower question. Three traders lost about $25 million when trades ran in a different order from the one the brothers’ validator had signed.

Related: BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF snaps $2.35B outflow streak amid extreme fear

To prove fraud, prosecutors had to show that signing the proposed block amounted to a promise to publish the trades in that order. They couldn’t establish what terms the brothers had accepted from the service that sent them the block.

That gap in the evidence helps explain the value of a provision in BlackRock’s own staking agreement. When the fund wants validators to maintain controls for screening sanctioned wallets, Coinbase must get a binding commitment from them. If a validator breaks that promise, the fund can point to a duty the validator accepted and ask Coinbase to enforce it.
